BEFORE THE PUBLIC SERVICE COMMISSION
                              OF THE STATE OF MISSOURI

In the Matter of Evergy Metro, Inc. d/b/a Evergy            )
Missouri Metro’s Request for Authority to Implement         )        File No. ER-2026-0143
a General Rate Increase for Electric Service                )

                 STAFF OBJECTION TO LLPS PARTIAL STIPULATION AND AGREEMENT

             COMES NOW the Staff (“Staff”) of the Missouri Public Service Commission

     (“Commission”), by and through counsel, and for its Objection to LLPS Partial Stipulation

     and Agreement respectfully states as follows:

            1.     On October 5, 2026, Evergy Missouri Metro, Inc. d/b/a Evergy Missouri Metro

    (“EMM”) and Google LLC (“Google”) filed their LLPS 1 Stipulation and Agreement

    (“Agreement”) resolving certain pending issues in this docket.

            2.     That same day, the Commission issued its Order Shortening Time to Object to

    Stipulation and Agreements, directing the parties to file any objections no later than midnight

    on October 7, 2026.

            3.     Pursuant to the Commission’s order and Commission Rule 20 CSR 4240-2.115,

    Staff objects to the Agreement reached between EMM and Google. In addition, Staff requests

    the opportunity to provide live testimony from Staff witnesses Sarah Lange, Brooke

    Mastrogiannis, and Kim Bolin in response to the Agreement.

                                  I.   Earnings Sharing Mechanism

            4.     Staff objects to the Earnings Review Mechanism (“ERM”) on page 2, paragraph 3

    of the Agreement. If the Commission decides an earning sharing mechanism is proper in this

    case, it should instead order the same mechanism approved by the Commission for


1
    Large Load Power Service.
                                                  1
 Ameren Missouri in Case No. ET-2025-0184.

         5.      Staff requests an opportunity for Kim Bolin, Financial and Business Analysis

Director, to provide live testimony in opposition to the ERM agreed to between

EMM and Google.

                                   II.   LLPS Billing Demand

         6.      The Agreement also addresses LLPS Billing Demand on page 2, paragraphs 4

and 5.        Staff objects to what it understands the LLPS billing calculation provisions to

represent, which is not the proper calculation of the LLPS minimum bill. Further Staff objects

to the LLPS Billing Demand in paragraph 4 because the tariff redlines promised in paragraph

5 to reflect the terms in the LLPS tariff have not been provided to Staff. Staff requests an

opportunity for Staff witness Sarah Lange, Economist, to provide live testimony in opposition

to the LLPS Billing Demand agreed to between EMM and Google.

                                           III.       FAC

         7.      Staff objects to the failure of the Agreement to properly modify the

Fuel Adjustment Clause (“FAC”) to protect ratepayers from adverse FAC impacts of

unprecedented customer growth, and the failure of the Agreement to mitigate or eliminate

EMM’s double-recovery (through the FAC and the LLPS energy charge) of energy expense to

serve LLPS customers which results in unreasonable positive regulatory lag. The design

contemplated by the Agreement does not reflect any LLPS energy kWh or energy expense in

the FAC base factor calculation.          Staff’s recommended base factor for Option 1

(which includes LLPS kWh and LLPS energy expense,) is $0.02030 per kWh.

Staff’s recommended base factor for Option 2 (which excludes LLPS from the FAC to the

extent practicable) is $0.01901. The stipulated FAC base factor is $0.01742. All else being
                                                  2
 equal, the lower the FAC base factor, the higher future FAC charges will be. An artificially low

base factor will compound the concerns Staff presented in its prefiled testimony related to

socialization of LLPS energy expense recovery through the FAC. Staff requests an opportunity

for Ms. Lange and Brooke Mastrogiannis, Regulatory Compliance Manager, to provide live

testimony in opposition to the FAC provisions of the Agreement.

        8.   Further, the approach specified in paragraph 7 and paragraph 9 is a far worse

deal for ratepayers, and benefits EMM more than any other approach provided by any party in

this proceeding for the following reasons:

             a.     The failure to include any LLPS energy in the FAC base factor calculation

             allows EMM to unreasonably double-recover all LLPS energy expense; and

             b.     The 90%/10% LLPS sharing mechanism does not provide real value for

             ratepayers. The 10% share would not be calculated as the total cost of energy

             for the LLPS class, or the difference between the energy expense included in the

             FAC base factor and that actually incurred. Instead, it would simply be a

             prorated share of the accumulated NET energy expense. For example, if LLPS

             was responsible for 50% of all EMM energy sales, the 10% share would equate

             to an overall sharing percentage of 92.5%/7/5%. The impotence of the 90%/10%

             sharing mechanism is demonstrated in Attachment A (Public).

   9. Paragraph 10 of the Agreement misrepresents the FAC base factor as coming from

       Staff by referencing the use of the net fuel costs included in Staff’s True-Up EMS run

       and using Staff’s NSI from Staff’s FAC base rate calculation. Staff’s base factor

       calculation excludes LLPS energy and related energy expenses, and it is not

       reasonable for use in a base factor calculation that includes LLPS energy and related
                                              3
        energy expenses in the Actual Net Energy Cost calculation.

   10. Staff objects to the inclusion of the subaccounts identified in paragraph 11 as

       improper. Evergy Missouri Metro’s long term capacity sales will fall off after the

       expected rates of this case, and Evergy Missouri Metro will add in long term capacity

       purchases after the expected rates of this case. If only one aspect is added in the base

       factor it is disproportionate to the reality of expected long term capacity in the future..

        11. The inclusion of long-term capacity within the FAC, as contemplated in

paragraph 11, will result in significant double-recovery for EMM.

        12. EMM currently sells its excess capacity to Evergy Missouri West, Inc. d/b/a

Evergy Missouri West (“EMW”). Those sales to EMW will taper off, just as EMM requires that

capacity for satisfaction of the resource adequacy requirements of its growing LLPS load.

The result of this situation is that currently, EMM is selling capacity to an affiliate at a

particular rate. In the near future, EMM will be using that capacity to meet customer

demands, and that customer demand will be providing revenues of over $20 per kW-month,

which is significantly higher than the revenue currently received per kW-month from EMW.

Despite earning more revenue from the same capacity (now through retail rates rather than a

capacity transaction) EMM is requesting further compensation for the drop off of the capacity

transaction through its FAC. The FAC was never contemplated for such use, and will require

ratepayers paying increased FAC costs.

        13. If the LLPS rates are not sufficient to recover incremental capacity expense from

LLPS customers, then EMM has the available regulatory tool of the LLPS interim capacity

charge. If EMM does not prudently pursue recovery through an LLPS interim capacity charge,

then EMM’s failure to recover should not be borne by EMM legacy ratepayers.
                                               4
         14. Paragraph 13 of the agreement outlines an amount of LLPS revenues and kWh

to be used in determining the revenue requirement in this case. However, those revenue

values rely on improper bill calculation and unreasonably low kWh amounts. Staff relied on

known contract demand and EMM’s representation of expected load factor to generate more

accurate outcomes as seen in Attachment B (HC).

        15. Staff further objects because the Agreement does not include the reasonable

reporting requirements recommended by Claire Eubanks, Industry Analysis Director.

The Agreement fails to reasonably resolve fairly straightforward issues such as annual

reporting to the Commission, enforcing the minimum bill provisions ordered by the

Commission in Case No. EO-2025-0154, enforcing the contract demand provisions ordered

by the Commission in Case No. EO-2025-0154, exempting the LLPS class from paying a FAC

charge, and ordering an equal percentage increase to the LLPS rate class when compared to

the other rate classes.

      WHEREFORE, Staff respectfully requests the Commission accept this objection, and

further not approve the LLPS Partial Stipulation and Agreement as a resolution to the

LLPS issues.
